newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya business leaders see polls as cure to chaos.
newsitem.headline: Kenya business leaders see polls as cure to chaos.

text.p: Business leaders urged the government of President Daniel arap Moi on Friday to fix an early date for elections to decide Kenya's destiny and calm local markets.
Presidential and parliamentary elections in which Moi, 73 and ruler since 1978, will seek a final five-year term, are due later in the year. No date has been set.

"Violent unrest is a major concern for business. Business is scared of looting, breaking into stores. Investors like peace. The biggest loss is a perception by investors that this is not a secure place to invest," said Kenya business magnate Chris Kirubi.
"An early election would help, we would resolve the issues and Kenya would be out of the current situation," said Manu Chandaria, chairman of the Kenya Association of Manufacturers.
Opposition parties, human rights and church groups in the coalition National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) have demanded a minimum package of constitutional reforms before elections.

Nine people were killed in Kenya on Monday during the most violent clashes between police and protesters since a campaign in July 1990 that helped persuade Moi to allow multi-party politics. The protests continued until Wednesday.
The Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) intervened in the foreign exchange market on Friday to stem the shilling's fall on continued jitters after the unrest, Governor Micah Cheserem said.

Cheserem said the shilling rate versus the dollar had eased to as low as 61.50 for bids from around 55 at the beginning of the week. The central bank offered $19 million to the market and there were few takers, he said.
Chandaria said violent confrontations were sending the wrong signal to foreign investors and undermined four years of economic reforms.

He noted that gross domestic product (GDP) growth had grown from near zero percent in 1991 to 4.6 percent in 1996 and a forecast of 4.0 percent this year. Inflation is at around 11 percent, down from 101 percent at the height of poor economic management in 1991 and 1992.
Poor weather has already cast a shadow over production of tea and coffee, Kenya's leading export commodities, and has increased pressure on domestic markets.

"These are negative signs, negative signs at a time that we are relatively happy. The investment climate is about right and there have been positive economic changes in the last couple of years," added Chandaria.
Chandaria said political unrest was grounding businesses because there were few local buyers for manufactured products and financial institutions were more reluctant to give credit.

Kirubi, whose interests range from real estate to cosmetics manufacturing and express mail delivery, told Reuters that violence gave the impression Kenya was unstable and not fit for investment. He added the government was determined to see normalcy return.
Most businesses had already discounted political upheaval in their budgets this year after violence preceding the 1992 elections, he said.

Vimal Shah, managing director at palm oil dealers Bidco Oil Refineries Ltd, said the volatile situation would fizzle out because "nothing is fundamentally wrong with the economy and it is likely that both parties are going to talk."
"Macroeconomic policies are in place. (Political) sense will prevail in the end. This volatility is a short-term thing. Things will stabilise (in the coming days)," Shah added.
